doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Learning dynamics from his father and Oscar Peterson
summary: Eddie says he learned dynamics early from his songwriter father and admires playing soft with intense beat, as in Oscar Peterson's trio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I just was very impressed by watching the three of you — Rossano and Nicki and yourself, with dynamics last night. How and when did you learn the importance of that?

Oh very early. My dad was a piano player in a Dixieland/swing style. He loved ragtime but he couldn’t quite get the stride thing going. So it was just very great. And he wrote songs, he wrote hundreds of songs and arrangements. And so I grew up listening to music, okay, that had dynamics and had melodies and rhythm, sometimes, for his style, not so complex rhythms as I got into the drums and my rhythm expanded, to be able to do over the bar line and stuff. But until the day he died he could look at me and say, “stop screwing around and just play time.” You know? And so from my dad came my concept of the time and what the drummer did with the time. You know, music has — the definition of music has certain elements, you know, melody, harmony, timbre, rhythm, and I think dynamics kind of gets held out of that. And it’s a hugely important part, and it has been since, you know, classical music. You listen to a Beethoven symphony and you know it’s this grand thing and all of a sudden it’s down to a flute solo again.
So the dynamics is a huge part. And with Rossano on piano, he’s such a dynamic player. And his touch, even when he’s playing light, is really very accurate. I don’t know if you noticed it.
He plays soft, it’s unbelievable. And so Nicki and I try to capture that with him. Like all of a sudden, we’ll be playing something loud, and then the bottom just drops out. But yet

the intensity of the beat continues. And that’s a really difficult thing to do in music. I think it’s the hardest thing to do in music. I used to hear that with Oscar Peterson records, trio records with Ray Brown and Ed Thigpen. They’d be playing and all of a sudden the bottom would drop out and Oscar might be just playing one note. But the beat continued through. And that’s what really impressed me.
I love how — I know I physically will lean forward when that happens.
Because I’m listening so much harder, and all of a sudden it’s a great effect.
